chapter_title: Introduction to React Native & Setting Up the Environment
chapter_summary:
Welcome to the final module of our Meta Android Developer Professional Certificate! Up until now, we've focused exclusively on building applications natively for Android using Kotlin and Android Studio. While native development offers unparalleled performance and access to device-specific features, it often means maintaining separate codebases for Android and iOS, which can be time-consuming and resource-intensive. This is where cross-platform frameworks like React Native come into play. React Native, developed by Meta (formerly Facebook), allows developers to build truly native mobile applications using JavaScript and React. It doesn't render web views; instead, it compiles your JavaScript code into native UI components, giving your app the look, feel, and performance of a truly native application. This approach significantly speeds up development, reduces costs, and enables a single team to target multiple platforms.

The core idea behind React Native is "Learn once, write anywhere." This means if you're already familiar with React for web development, you'll find many concepts, like components, props, and state, directly transferable. However, instead of using HTML elements like `<div>` or `<span>`, React Native provides its own set of native components like `View`, `Text`, `Image`, and `Button` that map directly to their Android (and iOS) counterparts. This "bridge" between JavaScript and native code is what makes React Native so powerful, allowing your JavaScript logic to interact with native modules and APIs. While it offers incredible efficiency, it's important to understand its limitations. For highly complex, performance-critical applications that require deep integration with very specific native hardware features or cutting-edge platform APIs, native development might still be the preferred choice. However, for the vast majority of mobile applications, React Native provides an excellent balance of performance, development speed, and code reusability.

To begin our journey with React Native, we first need to set up our development environment. The primary tools you'll need are Node.js (which includes npm, the Node package manager) and a code editor like VS Code. React Native projects are built using JavaScript, so Node.js is essential for running the JavaScript runtime outside of a browser. You can download Node.js from its official website; it's recommended to use the LTS (Long Term Support) version. Once Node.js is installed, you'll have access to `npm` (or `yarn`, another popular package manager). Next, you'll need to install either the Expo CLI or the React Native CLI. Expo is a set of tools and services built around React Native that significantly simplifies development, especially for beginners. It handles many complexities like native module linking and build processes, allowing you to focus purely on JavaScript. The Expo Go app on your phone allows you to instantly preview your app by scanning a QR code.

For more advanced scenarios or when you need to integrate custom native modules, the React Native CLI offers more control but requires a deeper understanding of native build tools (Android Studio, Xcode). For this course, we'll primarily focus on the Expo workflow as it's more beginner-friendly and allows for rapid prototyping. To install Expo CLI globally, open your terminal or command prompt and run `npm install -g expo-cli`. Once installed, you can create a new project using `expo init MyFirstReactNativeApp`. This command will prompt you to choose a template (e.g., `blank` for a minimal app). After the project is created and dependencies are installed, navigate into your project directory (`cd MyFirstReactNativeApp`) and start the development server with `npm start` or `expo start`. This will open a Metro Bundler interface in your browser, displaying a QR code.

Running your React Native application is straightforward. If you're using Expo, you can download the Expo Go app from the Google Play Store on your Android device or emulator. Once installed, simply scan the QR code displayed by the Metro Bundler, and your app will load instantly. This hot-reloading feature is one of React Native's greatest strengths, allowing for rapid iteration and testing. If you prefer to use an Android emulator, ensure you have Android Studio installed and an emulator configured, as we did for native Android development. When you run `expo start`, the Metro Bundler interface will also provide options to "Run on Android device/emulator." Clicking this will attempt to launch your app on an available emulator or a physical device connected via USB with debugging enabled. It's crucial to ensure your development machine and your physical device are on the same Wi-Fi network for the QR code scanning to work correctly. Common mistakes at this stage often involve firewall issues blocking communication or incorrect Node.js/npm installations. Always check the terminal output for error messages and consult the official React Native or Expo documentation for troubleshooting steps. Setting up the environment correctly is the foundation for a smooth development experience, so take your time and ensure everything is working as expected before moving on.

screens.title: Introduction to React Native & Environment Setup
screens.subtitle: Build native mobile apps with JavaScript, faster iteration, and a single codebase for Android and iOS.

narration.text: Welcome. In this chapter you'll learn what React Native is, why teams use it, and how to get a development environment ready so you can run your first app. React Native is a framework that lets you write application logic in JavaScript and React, but it renders to native UI components so apps feel and perform like native builds. That reduces duplicate work when targeting both Android and iOS and speeds development with hot reloading. To follow along you only need Node. js, a code editor like V S Code, and either Expo CLI for a managed, beginner-friendly experience or the React Native CLI for more control. We'll emphasize the Expo workflow because it simplifies native linking and lets you preview instantly with the Expo Go app. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to initialize a new project, start the Metro bundler, and run the app on an Android emulator or a device. Keep an eye out for common setup pitfalls like mismatched Node versions, firewall or network problems, and emulator configuration—these are the things that slow you down most. Ready to build your first cross-platform app?

screens.title: What is React Native?
screens.subtitle: A definition and a concrete example of how JavaScript becomes native UI

narration.text: React Native is a framework that enables you to write application code in JavaScript and React while rendering native platform UI components at runtime. In practice this means you author components and structure similar to web React, but instead of H T M L elements you use React Native primitives like View, Text, Image, and Button. Those primitives are not web views; they map to Android and iOS platform widgets so apps feel native. A concrete example: a Text component renders using the platform's native text control so fonts, line height, and accessibility behaviors match the device. A common misconception is to think React Native is a web app wrapped inside a mobile shell; it's not. The JavaScript runs on a separate JavaScript thread and communicates across a bridge to native modules when needed. That bridge is powerful but can be a performance factor if you shuffle large amounts of data across too often. Key takeaways: React Native accelerates cross-platform development, but you should design components with native rendering and bridge costs in mind. Consider whether your app needs tight native integration or benefits more from single-codebase speed before choosing this approach.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: React Native maps JavaScript components to native UI primitives so apps render using platform widgets, not web views.

content.html:
Core Concept › What is React Native?
React Native — core idea
A framework that compiles your JavaScript and React components into native UI elements on each platform.
How it works
  • Write components with primitives like View and Text that map to native widgets.
  • JavaScript logic runs and communicates with native modules via a bridge when needed.
  • Metro Bundler serves your JavaScript during development and enables hot reload for fast iteration.
Common misconception
Not a web app inside a shell — native rendering is used, though the JS-to-native bridge must be managed for heavy data flows.
Metaphor
Think of React Native as a translator: your JavaScript describes UI and behavior, and React Native speaks the platform's native UI language for each device.
Concrete example
A simple label
When you render a Text component, Android uses native text rendering and iOS uses its own text control. Styling looks consistent but behaves like a native control on each platform.
Key Takeaway

React Native gives native UI performance while letting you build in JavaScript, but assess bridge costs for heavy data operations.

screens.title: Native Components & the Bridge
screens.subtitle: How View, Text, and Image map to platform widgets and how the JavaScript-to-native bridge works

narration.text: Understanding native components and the bridge is essential. React Native provides primitives like View, Text, Image, and Button that directly map to platform widgets — not browser elements. This mapping means layout, accessibility, and native behaviors are provided by each platform’s UI system. The JavaScript you write runs in a JavaScript runtime and communicates with native modules via a bridge. This allows your layout and logic to be implemented in JavaScript while leveraging native performance for rendering. A concrete example: when you call a native camera A P I from JavaScript, the request crosses the bridge to a native module that opens the camera UI. A common misconception is believing the bridge is free; excessive synchronous calls or sending large payloads across the bridge can become a bottleneck. To avoid this, batch updates where possible or write native modules for heavy processing. Key takeaway: design with fewer round trips across the bridge for smoother performance, and use native modules thoughtfully when you need platform-specific functionality. Native Components & the Bridge means native primitives render with platform controls; the bridge enables js-to-native interaction but can be a performance consideration if overused.. In practical terms, how view, text, and image map to platform widgets and how the javascript-to-native bridge works. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Architecture insight
keyIdea.text: Native primitives render with platform controls; the bridge enables JS-to-native interaction but can be a performance consideration if overused.

content.html:
Definition › Native Components & Bridge
Native primitives
View, Text, Image map to the platform's UI building blocks so behavior and appearance match native apps.
Architecture overview
  • JavaScript thread: runs your app logic and component lifecycle.
  • Native thread: performs rendering and platform UI operations.
  • Bridge: asynchronous channel for commands and data between JS and native modules.
Misconception
The bridge is invisible cost-free plumbing — actually, heavy or synchronous bridge use can degrade performance.
Example: invoking a native API
When a JavaScript call requests the camera, the command goes over the bridge to a native module that presents the camera UI. The image result is sent back across the bridge to JavaScript.
Performance guidance
  1. Minimize frequent synchronous calls across the bridge.
  2. Batch updates and use native animations for smooth visuals.
  3. When heavy processing is needed, consider a native module.
Key Takeaway

The bridge enables powerful native integration, but design to reduce crossing it for best app responsiveness.

screens.title: Expo CLI vs React Native CLI
screens.subtitle: Choose the right workflow: managed convenience versus native control

narration.text: Choosing between Expo CLI and the React Native CLI is about trade-offs. Expo CLI provides a managed workflow that abstracts native build complexity, handles linking for many common native modules, and offers the Expo Go app to preview your project instantly by scanning a QR code. This makes Expo ideal for rapid prototyping, learning, and many production apps that rely on supported native features. React Native CLI offers direct access to native projects and build tools, requiring manual configuration in Android Studio and Xcode, but it gives you full control when you need custom native modules or deeper platform integration. A concrete example: if you need a very specific native SDK not supported by Expo, the React Native CLI or a bare workflow is appropriate. A common misconception is that Expo cannot produce production apps — it can, but some advanced native features may require ejecting to the bare workflow. Key takeaway: start with Expo to validate ideas quickly and move to the CLI only when you need native-level customization. Expo CLI vs React Native CLI means expo = fast, managed, great for prototyping; react native cli = full native control for custom modules and platform-specific needs.. In practical terms, choose the right workflow: managed convenience versus native control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Workflow trade-off
keyIdea.text: Expo = fast, managed, great for prototyping; React Native CLI = full native control for custom modules and platform-specific needs.

content.html:
Comparison › Expo CLI vs React Native CLI
Expo CLI (managed)
  • Simplifies setup and native linking for many common APIs.
  • Use Expo Go to preview without building native binaries.
  • Great for rapid prototyping and beginner workflows.
Misconception: Expo cannot be used for production — in many cases it can, but very specialized native features may require ejecting.
React Native CLI (bare)
  • Generates native Android and iOS projects you can open in platform IDEs.
  • Required when adding custom native modules or deep native SDKs.
  • Requires installing Android Studio and Xcode for full native builds.
Use case example: integrating a platform SDK with native-only bindings.
When to pick Expo
Prototype quickly, preview on devices, and avoid native build complexity.
When to pick CLI
Need custom native modules or deep integrations with platform SDKs.
Practical tip
Start with Expo. Move to CLI when you outgrow the managed workflow.

screens.title: Install Node.js and Tools
screens.subtitle: Prepare the environment: Node.js, npm, code editor, Android Studio (emulator)

narration.text: Before creating a React Native project, set up the required tools. Start by installing Node. js, preferably the LTS release, which includes npm — the Node package manager. A code editor such as V S Code is recommended for editing JavaScript and project configuration. If you plan to run an Android emulator, install Android Studio and configure an emulator image as you would for native Android development. For Expo-focused work you don’t need Xcode, but Android Studio is still useful for emulators. After Node is installed, confirm npm or yarn works by running a simple package list command in your terminal. A common mistake is using an unsupported Node version or having multiple Node installations that confuse the system PATH. Also check that Android Studio's command-line tools are available if you want to start an emulator from the terminal. Key takeaway: a correct, consistent toolchain avoids time-consuming errors later, so verify Node, npm, and emulator availability before initializing projects. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Install Expo CLI and Initialize a Project
screens.subtitle: Terminal-first demo of global install, project initialization, and starting Metro Bundler

narration.text: Now we perform the commands that create and start an Expo project. Begin by installing the Expo CLI globally through your package manager so you can run its init command. After that, run the project initialization flow which prompts you to choose a template; choose a minimal or blank template for this course. Once the project files install, change into the new directory and start the development server which launches the Metro bundler. A concrete example of the workflow is: install Expo CLI globally, run the initialization command to create MyFirstReactNativeApp, then navigate into the folder and start. A common mistake is not having global install permissions or mixing npm and yarn installs that could cause inconsistent node modules. Another frequent issue is not opening the terminal in the project directory before starting the bundler. When you start Metro, it will display a QR code you can scan with Expo Go or use to attach an emulator. Key takeaway: follow the terminal output — it reports missing dependencies and instructions to fix them. content.html:
Process › Install Expo CLI & init
Commands (example)
Run these in your terminal. If you use yarn, substitute the package manager commands accordingly.
npm install -g expo-cli
expo init MyFirstReactNativeApp
cd MyFirstReactNativeApp
npm start
If global install fails due to permissions, consider using a node version manager or run with appropriate elevated permissions on your OS.
What Metro Bundler shows
  • A QR code to scan with Expo Go.
  • Options to run on Android emulator, web, or to publish.
  • Terminal output with errors and dependency warnings.
Common mistake
Running start in the wrong directory or missing node modules — always cd into the project folder before starting the server.
Key Takeaway

The terminal guides you: follow its instructions, address permission or dependency warnings, and then scan the QR code to preview.

screens.title: Run Your App on Expo Go or an Emulator
screens.subtitle: From Metro QR code to the app launching on an Android device or emulator

narration.text: With Metro Bundler running, you can preview your app two common ways. First, use the Expo Go app on a physical Android device: open Expo Go, scan the QR code displayed by Metro, and your JavaScript bundle will be loaded into the app. This is fast and requires no native builds. Second, run on an Android emulator configured in Android Studio. In the Metro interface there is an option to launch on Android device/emulator — this attempts to start the app on any running emulator or connected device with debugging enabled. A practical example: start Metro, open Android Studio and launch a virtual device, then choose 'Run on Android' in Metro. Common pitfalls include missing ADB setup or the device and development machine not sharing the same network for QR scanning. Also ensure USB debugging is enabled for physical devices. Key takeaway: Expo Go is the quickest path to preview; emulators are useful for deeper device testing and when a physical device is not available. Run Your App on Expo Go or an Emulator means use expo go to scan the metro qr for instant preview, or launch a configured android emulator for a fuller device simulation.. In practical terms, from metro qr code to the app launching on an android device or emulator. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Run & Preview
keyIdea.text: Use Expo Go to scan the Metro QR for instant preview, or launch a configured Android emulator for a fuller device simulation.

content.html:
Process Flow › Run on Expo Go or Emulator
Expo Go (physical device)
Install Expo Go from your app store. With Metro running, scan the QR code and your project loads instantly with hot reload.
Checklist
  • Device and dev machine on same Wi-Fi network for QR preview.
  • Expo Go running on the device while scanning the QR.
  • Check terminal output for bundler status.
Android emulator
Open Android Studio, start a virtual device, and then select 'Run on Android device/emulator' in Metro or trigger adb to install the bundle.
Common pitfalls
  • ADB not on PATH or emulator not running.
  • Firewall blocking bundle requests for physical device preview.
  • Not enabling USB debugging for a connected device.
Key Takeaway

Expo Go is the fastest preview route. Emulators are essential when you need to simulate device variants and debug native behaviors.

screens.title: Metro Bundler & Hot Reload
screens.subtitle: What Metro does and why hot reload speeds development

narration.text: Metro Bundler is the JavaScript bundler used by React Native. During development it serves your JavaScript bundle, watches for file changes, and enables hot reloading so you can see UI updates without restarting the app. In practice Metro runs when you start the development server and shows a QR code plus run options; it also prints useful diagnostic logs to the terminal. A concrete workflow: edit App. js, save, and Metro recompiles the changed modules and pushes updates to the running app — that is hot reload. Misconceptions include thinking hot reload is always instantaneous for large projects; large dependency graphs may take longer to recompile. When hot reload does not reflect changes, check for bundler errors in the terminal, ensure the device is connected to the same network, and verify that development mode is enabled. Key takeaway: Metro and hot reload form the rapid edit-test loop that makes React Native productive; keeping your bundler healthy and watching terminal output prevents many delays. Metro Bundler & Hot Reload means metro serves and recompiles javascript during development. hot reload pushes ui changes for rapid iteration; check terminal logs when updates fail.. In practical terms, what metro does and why hot reload speeds development. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Developer loop
keyIdea.text: Metro serves and recompiles JavaScript during development. Hot reload pushes UI changes for rapid iteration; check terminal logs when updates fail.

content.html:
Definition › Metro Bundler & Hot Reload
Metro: the development server
Metro watches files, bundles JavaScript, and serves it to the running app with hot reload support.
Timeline of a change
Edit
You save a change in App.js.
Recompile
Metro rebuilds the affected module bundle.
Push
Hot reload applies the update to the running app.
Troubleshooting hints
  • Inspect terminal logs for bundler errors.
  • Confirm the device can reach the bundler (network or USB debug).
  • Restart Metro if stale caches cause inconsistent updates.

screens.title: Common Pitfalls & Troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: Network, Node, and emulator issues that block progress and how to fix them

narration.text: Setup problems are the most common source of frustration. Typical issues include mismatched Node versions, global install permission errors, blocked network connections, and emulator configuration mistakes. For example, a global install can fail if your terminal lacks permission to write to global folders — solutions include using a node version manager or running with appropriate privileges. Network problems often prevent Expo Go from scanning the QR code; ensure both devices share the same Wi-Fi and check for firewall rules. Emulator issues often stem from ADB not being on the PATH or the virtual device not being started in Android Studio. A misconception is blaming React Native for problems that are actually environmental; always read the terminal output first. Concrete troubleshooting steps: check Node and npm versions, restart Metro, verify emulator state in Android Studio, and test Expo Go with a simple network ping to the dev machine. Key takeaway: focused diagnostic checks of the terminal, environment variables, and device connectivity will resolve most setup failures quickly. screens.title: When to Choose Native vs React Native
screens.subtitle: A decision guide for performance, platform APIs, and team trade-offs

narration.text: Deciding between native development and React Native is a strategic choice. React Native excels when you want faster development cycles, code reuse across Android and iOS, and rapid prototyping with hot reload. However, native development remains the right choice for apps that demand maximum performance for graphics-heavy experiences, require exclusive access to the newest platform APIs, or when fine-tuned memory and threading control is mandatory. A concrete scenario: if you're building a simple business app with forms and lists, React Native offers a big productivity gain. If you're building a high-frame-rate game or an app that depends on a specialized hardware SDK, native Android with Kotlin may be more appropriate. A common misconception is that React Native always reduces cost — while it often lowers initial development effort, long-term requirements for platform-specific features can reintroduce native work. Key takeaway: evaluate features, performance needs, and team skills before committing to either approach and consider prototyping in React Native to validate feasibility quickly. Pro Tip › When to choose Native vs React Native
Decision guide
Compare project needs against the strengths of each approach.
Choose React Native when:
  • You need rapid iteration and code reuse across platforms.
  • Your app uses standard UI patterns and common native modules.
  • You want to prototype quickly with Expo.
Choose native when:
  • Maximum platform performance or specialized hardware APIs are required.
  • You must use a native-only SDK or need deep platform integration.
Practical tip: prototype in React Native to validate whether performance and integration meet your needs before committing to a full native rewrite.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential ideas you should remember. First, React Native is a framework that allows you to write JavaScript and React components and render them as native UI elements, giving you native-like behavior without writing platform-specific UI code for each OS. Second, Expo CLI is a beginner-friendly managed workflow that simplifies development by providing the Expo Go preview app and handling many native details, while the React Native CLI provides fuller native control when you need custom modules. Third, Metro Bundler serves your JavaScript during development and hot reload enables rapid iteration so you can see changes without rebuilding. Keep these three concepts in mind as you set up your environment and begin building. Each is a building block for fast cross-platform development and for choosing the right workflow for your project's needs.
